Mon 15 Jun 2026 at 5:27pm

By Courtney Gould

Thanks for sticking with us. We'll be back bright and early tomorrow morning for another day on the federal politics live blog.

You can look back at today's developments below, or download the ABC News app and subscribe to our range of news alerts for the latest updates.

Mon 15 Jun 2026 at 5:11pm

By Courtney Gould

Australia's mineral exploration sector should be carved out from the government's capital gains tax changes, an industry body says.

Warren Pierce, the chief executive of the Association of Mining and Exploration Companies (AMEC), describes the industry as the "original start up" and says it relies on mum and dad retail investors "taking a punt on their success".

"Mineral exploration already relies on a very small and shrinking pool of retail investors. Risk capital is hard to come by, and if mum and dad retail investors desert mineral exploration, there will be no investment to replace," he says.

He does his best to link the sweeping tax change to yesterday's Socceroos win over Türkiye.

"As last night's match against Türkiye shows, Australia has a history of winning against the odds. But if government persists with these CGT changes, it could be the greatest economic own goal our country ever scores."

Mon 15 Jun 2026 at 4:39pm

By Courtney Gould

Business Council of Australia's Bran Black has taken aim at the timeframe the government has placed on passing sweeping changes to the capital gains tax and negative gearing.

The bill is currently being examined by a two-day Senate inquiry, with the government hoping to pass the legislation before parliament rises for the winter break on July 2.

Black contrasted this to an inquiry about the removal of so-called nuisance tariffs (tariffs that don't raise much revenue and cost more to administer than they're worth) that ran for nine months.

"I think the fundamental challenge that we've got in terms of these reforms and the process so far is the timing associated with the way in which it's proceeding," he says.

"We've got effectively 22 days of inquiry with respect to these reforms and about a year ago, we had nine months of inquiry into the question as to whether or not we should remove nuisance tariffs on mushrooms, yam and horsehair.

"So it seems to me that given these changes are described as the most consequential tax changes in a quarter of a century, there is more time that is required in order to consider them properly."

COSBOA says they have met with Treasury and ministers to ventilate their concerns. Chair Matthew Addison "believe they've listened" but COSBOA haven't "got a feedback loop at this time".

All three organisations said they had not been asked by the government to sign an NDA during discussions.

Mon 15 Jun 2026 at 4:31pm

By Courtney Gould

A trio of business groups has begun their appearance at a two-day Senate inquiry into the government's proposed tax changes.

It's safe to say the Council of Small Business Organisations Australia (COSBOA), Business Council of Australia (BCA) and the Australian Chamber of Commerce and Industry (ACCI) are not fans of the changes.

COSBA remains concerned changes to the capital gains tax discount will disincentive small business growth. Chief executive Skye Cappuccio reiterated the turnover threshold for exemptions was "outdated" and should be raised from $2m to $10m

ACCI's David Alexander says there "is no compelling economic reason why tax reform should require higher taxes on investment in businesses".

BCA's Bran Black says the council does not support the bill or the process surrounding it.

"The BCA participated in the economic reform roundtable with a clear position that any tax reform must increase business investment. This bill does not meet that test," he says.

"This is not the kind of tax reform that is needed to grow the pie, to lift investments, wages, and living standards."

Mon 15 Jun 2026 at 3:20pm

By Pablo Viñales

Housing groups,  including the Property Council of Australia, Housing Industry Association and Master Builders Australia have addressed the Senate inquiry into the federal government’s sweeping changes to negative gearing and capital gains.

Earlier, former ACCC chair, Graeme Samuel, told the inquiry "vested interests" had "submerged" the tax debate.

Property council chief executive Mike Zorbas has hit back at that comment.

"Property organisations in particular are not anything other than invested interests, they're not vested interests. They are directly invested in the prosperity of Australia," he said.

Zorbas also told the inquiry the changes would shrink housing supply and he took aim at the federal government over its economic roundtable last year.

"Government overspending at federal and state levels by all parties and a lack of actual reform, think GST amongst other taxes, has left us taxing the life out of  new property projects and existing operating assets at a time of rising capital, rising Labor and construction costs.

"Taken as the sum of its outputs, last year's Economic Reform Roundtable now appears to be a tax hike forum."

Mon 15 Jun 2026 at 3:09pm

By Courtney Gould

Opposition Leader Angus Taylor is asked what he is doing to combat the rise of One Nation and if he's worried by the results of recent opinion polls.

"I'll tell you what worries me. What worries me is how this government is trashing the country, taking us in the wrong direction," he sidesteps.

He says his real "fight" and "beef" is with the government, taking aim at the budget's impact on small business owners.

Taylor says he's "never seen such anger, absolute raw anger" at the government.

"They don't get it," he says.

Mon 15 Jun 2026 at 2:53pm

By Courtney Gould

Only a little while ago, Prime Minister Anthony Albanese indicated he's going to make a decision on whether to extend the fuel excise cut in the coming days.

The tax on fuel was reduced earlier this year amid the outbreak of hostilities in the Middle East. The move has saved motorists 26 cents per litre, but the temporary measure is due to end on June 30.

Opposition Leader Angus Taylor says he wants to see what happens to fuel prices "over the next little while".

"The crude oil price at least has come down overnight and we'd expect that to flow through to the bowser. But let's see if it's sustained," he says.

"We're clearly, potentially at a real turning point in what we're seeing in the Middle East, that has the potential to have a real impact. But we want to see lower prices at the bowser. I think that's what all Australians want to see."

Mon 15 Jun 2026 at 2:50pm

By Courtney Gould

Opposition Leader Angus Taylor has welcomed the ceasefire agreement between the United States and Iran.

"That is a good thing. We want the Strait of Hormuz opened up as fast as possible. That is good for all of us. It means it will bring down the price of fuel at the bowser. That is what we have all wanted to see," he says.

"We also want to see a peace deal, where the Iranian people are able to live their lives as they want to live them, but also that the rest of the world is secure and the nuclear capability that Iran has been building cannot be resumed."

Mon 15 Jun 2026 at 2:40pm

By Courtney Gould

Alrighty, we're heading to Alice Springs now where Opposition Leader Angus Taylor is holding a press conference at Central Petroleum alongside NT chief minister Lia Finocchiaro and Jacinta Nampijinpa Price.

Mon 15 Jun 2026 at 2:37pm

By Courtney Gould

Anthony Albanese is also asked, repeatedly, about One Nation and Pauline Hanson.

Hanson claims more than 65,000 Australians have contributed to One Nation over the past week.

So how will the PM fight against her claim that he's a liar?

"I talk about what I'm going to deliver for Australians and don't engage in the sort of personalised politics that we are seeing," he responds.

On the recent trend of polling in support of One Nation, Albanese is playing it cool. He notes that many of the polls in February last year had Peter Dutton winning the 2025 election.

"I encourage you to go and have a look and see how that stood up to the test of time, when people had to make a decision about who is in the best position to actually provide effective government," he says.

Mon 15 Jun 2026 at 2:32pm

By Courtney Gould

Anthony Albanese has reiterated disabled Australians would not be left without support as the government pushes ahead  with its reforms to the National Disability Insurance Scheme.

The overhaul was examined by a tight three-day inquiry last week with a report due to be handed down in the coming days. Advocate Hannah Diviney warned the inquiry that people could die under the changes.

The prime minister says the government would "make sure that people get assistance".

"It doesn't assist the process to unnecessarily concern people not based upon the facts," he says.

"We've made it very clear ... people won't be left without support."

Key Event

Mon 15 Jun 2026 at 2:26pm

By Courtney Gould

So with the end of the war in sight, what does that do to the government's thinking about extending the fuel excise cut?

The fuel excise was halved back in April in a bid to tackle high prices as a result of the closure in the Strait of Hormuz.

Albanese says the ceasefire agreement was only just announced, adding the government will continue to monitor the issue with a decision to be made in the coming days.

"We'll make an assessment over the coming period and we'll make an appropriate announcement. We know that the end of the conflict doesn't mean that we're back to business as usual. And we know that that has been really important in providing support for people," he says.

Albanese also notes the first round of tax cuts passed last year will come into effect on July 1, the same day the fuel excise is due to return to its normal rate.

The PM says the expenditure review committee is due to meet next week.

Mon 15 Jun 2026 at 2:21pm

By Courtney Gould

Prime Minister Anthony Albanese has also given a bit of a shout out to the Socceroos, who had a big win in their first World Cup match.

"An amazing game," he says, noting the team was "underestimated" before its game against Türkiye.

"It's fantastic that so many Australians have travelled to North America to cheer on the Australian Socceroos team. And we look forward to the games against the United States and Paraguay and then to the next round, where things are looking pretty, pretty hopeful that we'll reach there as well."

Key Event

Mon 15 Jun 2026 at 2:15pm

By Courtney Gould

Prime Minister Anthony Albanese has welcomed the agreement between the United States and Iran to end the war.

A ceasefire has been reached with both sides confirming plans to end fighting and reopen the Strait of Hormuz, with a signing ceremony expected in Switzerland on Friday.

But Albanese warns the war's impact will be felt for some time. The prime minister says he is also "very conscious" that the end of hostilities does not mean that everything returns to normal.

"It will be, at a minimum, many months before things return to normal," he says.

Albanese highlighted the work of Pakistan, Qatar, Saudi Arabia and Türkiye and their efforts in mediating a deal.

Mon 15 Jun 2026 at 2:09pm

By Courtney Gould

We're sticking with the housing theme today.

Prime Minister Anthony Albanese has his hard hat and fluoro vest on while visiting a development in Canberra's north alongside Andrew Leigh and Clare O'Neil.

I'll bring you updates as they come in.

Mon 15 Jun 2026 at 2:06pm

By Courtney Gould

Saul Eslake, an independent economist, has a couple of issues with the changes to the capital tax gains discount.

He wants other arrangements considered for start-ups and has concerns about the 30 per cent minimum tax rate and if those on lower income brackets would end up paying more tax after realising a capital gain.

Eslake also would like the government to reinstate averaging for people who are not regular recipients of capital gains, as was permitted from 1985 to 1999.

Asked if he thought the changes would improve housing supply and rental shocks, Eslake said it would improve the ability of would-be first time owners to become homeowners.

"So what matters for rents is that changes in net supply of housing, that is, gross supply of housing minus changes in the demand for it," he said.

"And I think the changes that are proposed in the budget will reduce the demand for rental housing by allowing more people to become homeowners."

Mon 15 Jun 2026 at 1:49pm

By Courtney Gould

Graeme Samuel, the former chamber of commerce president and former chair of the ACCC, has taken aim at the "private vested interests" that have "submerged" the debate on tax.

"The one thing that I have learned over all these 35 years is this: the measure of the public interest in relation to reform is generally in inverse proportion to the noise that is made by private vested interests," he told a Senate inquiry.

"The private vested interests have got very, very good megaphones, and they'll march up and down the street with their megaphones and their signs saying 'this is going to be a disaster, woe betide us'."

Saul Eslake, an independent economist who was also appearing at the inquiry, said the introduction of the 50 per cent capital gains tax discount in 1999 had not resulted in "any positive effects to Australia's economy performance".

"Nor did the changes to the CGT regime trigger a surge in productivity-enhancing business investment."

He said rather it "detracted from both economic and social policy objectives" and the CGT change was "undoubtedly" a significant contributor to the trend of housing unaffordability and decline in home ownership rates for people under 55.

Mon 15 Jun 2026 at 1:22pm

By Joshua Boscaini

The opposition leader has welcomed the ceasefire agreement between the US and Iran, but says the opposition wants to see the details.

In a statement, Angus Taylor says the agreement must be lasting, durable, enforceable and backed by action to keep the Strait of Hormuz open.

The Coalition says it's "deeply disappointing" the prime minister wasn't able to secure an invitation to this year's G7 Leaders Summit in France.

"At a time when decisions are being made that will affect Australian fuel prices, energy security and regional stability Australia should be at the table," Taylor says.

"The Coalition supports serious efforts to de-escalate the conflict, reopen the Strait of Hormuz and restore stability in the Middle East

"Australia must stand with our partners, defend freedom of navigation and protect Australians from the worst impacts of global instability."

Mon 15 Jun 2026 at 12:30pm

By Courtney Gould

University of Melbourne associate professor Kathryn James was also asked if start-ups should be carved out of the proposed changes to the capital gains discount.

The sector is concerned because of a low cost base (say a laptop at someone's kitchen table) means there is little purchase price to index to inflation, so investors lose a much greater tax benefit than traditional companies.

But James says once you start making exemptions it snowballs, and having a broad tax base is simpler.

"To me, it's defensible that if you've ... sold a profitable business then a tax of 30 per cent, once you've been able to deduct your losses, is reasonable and defensible," she said.

"Once we start introducing carve outs for certain sectors and certain industries then we can see what's happening in relation to this Senate committee ... everyone can make a claim case for special treatment, and it starts to snowball."

Mon 15 Jun 2026 at 12:16pm

By Courtney Gould

A tax academic has raised concerns the government's proposed housing tax changes could incentivise investors to turn towards self-managed superannuation funds as a loophole.

University of Melbourne associate professor Kathryn James told an inquiry into the proposed overhaul to the capital gains tax discount and negative gearing that further changes will need to be looked at.

"The reforms to discretionary trusts will be needed and will need to be forthcoming, and there will need to be a discussion had around the use of superannuation as a tax minimisation vehicle, as well, so cutting off other loopholes is important in that respect," she said.

She says she has concerns about SMSFs and the way super had "gone beyond" being a vehicle for retirement savings to a "tax-preferred investment vehicle".

"There is a need to close off those loopholes and that's a job for further down the line."

Overall, James said while the proposed changes were not perfect, they were appropriate to make the tax system fairer. She argued while some would call for the status quo to remain, the evidence was "weak" and high-income earners "generally try to avoid" paying more tax on capital income.
